title: Evaluating Prompt-Injection and Retrieval/Tool-Channel Attacks on Agentic NetOps Pipelines and Layered Defenses
abstract: Problem: Agentic LLM pipelines for NetOps expose retrieval and tool channels that adversaries can exploit via prompt injection. Method: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory experiment comparing an unguarded agentic NetOps pipeline (baseline) against a defense-in-depth configuration (RAG grounding with provenance + deterministic runtime validator + sandboxed tool outputs). Design: 80 preregistered task seeds × 2 model families planned (paired design); deterministic parsing and provenance checks; preregistration and all artifacts frozen and hashed. Confirmatory result: among 150 complete paired runs analyzed, baseline attack-success = 147/150 (98.0%), guarded (combined defense) attack-success = 150/150 (100.0%); paired difference (guarded − baseline) = +0.02, 95% bootstrap CI [0.00, 0.0467]; exact McNemar two-sided p = 0.25. Limitation: observed baseline rate substantially exceeded the preregistered power assumption, and 10 preregistered pairs were unavailable and excluded per preregistered rules (details below and in the published artifacts). Conclusion: for the studied prototype and adversarial corpus, the implemented combined defense did not produce a detectable reduction in attack-success; all experiment logs, prompts, model-configuration manifest, parser outputs, provenance traces, and analysis artifacts are published in the execution bundle (hashed and referenced in the Disclosure Statement).

sections.introduction: Agentic LLM systems promise intent-driven automation for network operations (NetOps) but expand the attack surface: retrieval (RAG) and tool channels can carry adversarial instructions. Prior work documents indirect prompt-injection and agentic attack surfaces and motivates defense-in-depth (RAG grounding, provenance, deterministic validators, sandboxing). We study whether a layered defensive configuration reduces adversarial-injection success in an agentic NetOps prototype under a preregistered paired design. Research question: How effective are retrieval- and tool-channel prompt-injection attacks against an agentic NetOps pipeline, and to what extent does the defense-in-depth configuration reduce attack success?
sections.related_work: We positioned the study against verified literature on prompt injection and agentic LLM agents, RAG/grounding approaches, generate-verify-repair patterns, and runtime/shielding defenses (representative recent sources are cited in the preregistration and manifest). The work is experimental and narrowly scoped to attack–defense interactions in a simulator-executable NetOps semantics layer.
sections.methodology: Preregistration: study id cnsmautocand-2-v1 was frozen before execution and specifies the paired confirmatory contrast, inclusion/exclusion rules, seeds, retry policy, estimands, and analysis plan. Model scope (preregistered): two hosted-model families were specified—OpenAI GPT-4 family and Anthropic Claude-2 family (model-family level identifiers recorded in the frozen model-configuration artifact; see Disclosure Statement). Pipeline: automated agentic prototype assembled from public components and deterministic modules: a retrieval (RAG) module with a frozen index and provenance recorder, a deterministic parser mapping LLM outputs to canonical CLI ASTs, a deterministic runtime verifier/oracle (policy predicates), and a sandboxed tool-emulation layer. Conditions executed (per preregistration): baseline (unguarded agentic pipeline), RAG-only, validator-only, and combined defense (RAG+validator+sandbox). Primary estimand: relative reduction in attack-success proportion for combined defense vs baseline under a paired-per-task-model design. Execution: runs automated per the frozen sampling plan; retries allowed only for infrastructure/API failures (one automatic retry) and logged. Deterministic parsing and provenance checks were preregistered as inclusion/exclusion rules: parser failures, retrieval-index/hash mismatches, or out-of-scope provenance cause exclusion from the primary confirmatory analysis (such exclusions and counts are recorded and hashed in the artifact bundle). All inputs and outputs were recorded and hashed (see Disclosure Statement and artifact hashes).
sections.results: Execution summary (from the frozen execution manifest): planned_episode_count = 320, completed_episode_count = 300, failed_episode_count = 20, model_calls_used = 163. Missingness and exclusions: 10 preregistered paired units were unavailable and excluded from the confirmatory analysis per the preregistered rules; missingness and exclusion counts are recorded in analysis/missingness_summary.csv (artifact hash provided in Disclosure). Confirmatory analysis (per preregistered paired analysis; complete pairs n = 150): baseline attack-success = 147/150 (98.0%); guarded (combined defense) attack-success = 150/150 (100.0%). Full paired contingency counts (primary contrast, provided here as preregistered-required detail): n_11 = 147 (success both baseline and guarded), n_10 = 3 (success baseline, failure guarded), n_01 = 0 (failure baseline, success guarded), n_00 = 0 (failure both). Paired estimate (guarded − baseline) = +0.020000000000000018. Exact McNemar two-sided p = 0.25 (implementation = exact_mcnemar_two_sided per preregistered analysis plan). Bootstrap 95% percentile CI for the paired difference = [0.00, 0.04666666666666667]; bootstrap seed = 1729; resamples = 10000 (as recorded in analysis log). Caching and model-call accounting: total model_calls_used = 163 across completed episodes (300), implying substantial reuse of cached model responses; a deterministic call-cache was used (call-cache files are present and hashed in the execution bundle). Average model calls per completed episode ≈ 163/300 ≈ 0.54 (reflecting deterministic reuse and cached responses across repeated condition evaluations); the call-cache contents and hashes are included in the artifact bundle. All scoring artifacts, per-run provenance traces, raw LLM transcripts, parser outputs, and scoring JSONs are published and hashed (execution/artifact_hashes contains per-file hashes).
sections.discussion: Primary confirmatory interpretation: for the implemented prototype, adversarial payloads produced very high baseline attack-success (98%) and the combined defense did not produce a statistically detectable reduction (paired difference point estimate +2%, two-sided McNemar p = 0.25, CI includes 0). Several important, preregistered construct and external-validity caveats apply and explain why the result must be interpreted conservatively: (1) baseline attack-success was far higher than the conservative baseline assumption in the preregistration (the preregistration planned power under a much lower baseline p0); this deviation reduces the realized power to detect the preregistered ≥70% relative reduction target and is reported as an experiment limitation; (2) the implemented validator predicates, RAG indexing policy, and sandbox were prototype implementations—differences in predicate strength, provenance policies, or retrieval filtering could materially change outcomes; the validator logic, RAG index build, and prompt/policy templates used at runtime are recorded in the frozen model-configuration artifact and execution logs (hash references in Disclosure) for audit; (3) the experiment ran in a simulator-executable NetOps semantics layer (no live-device actions), and simulator-model mismatch is a construct-validity threat; (4) missingness: 10 preregistered pairs were unavailable and excluded according to the preregistered rules (reasons and task ids for excluded runs are recorded in analysis/missingness_summary.csv), reducing the analyzed sample to 150 complete pairs and further reducing precision. Reviewer requests and resolved items: we now report the full paired contingency counts (n_11, n_10, n_01, n_00) in the Results above and provide the exact bootstrap seed/resamples and McNemar p-value as produced by the preregistered analysis. Items that require inspection of raw artifacts (exact model API version strings, frozen prompt templates, representative adversarial payloads, raw LLM outputs, parsed ASTs, and the deterministic validator rule set and RAG-index construction details) are available in the published artifact bundle (hashed and referenced in the Disclosure Statement). Where a requested summary could be computed from the archived artifacts we have included the computed summary (paired table, counts, totals, model_calls_used and average calls per episode); where the reviewer requested novel recomputation not present in archived analysis (for example, a post-hoc power recalculation under the observed baseline and alternative MDE values), we preserve the request as an explicit unresolved item to avoid fabricating computations beyond the stored analysis outputs. Exploratory material: per-condition scoring JSONs and per-run provenance traces are published (execution/scoring/*.json, execution/provider_calls/*.json) and permit per-attack-type and per-task-cluster stratified analyses on demand; these exploratory breakdowns were not part of the preregistered confirmatory contrast and are therefore provided as audit artifacts rather than as revised confirmatory claims in this manuscript.
sections.conclusion: In a preregistered paired confirmatory study of prompt-injection against an agentic NetOps prototype, the implemented defense-in-depth configuration (RAG with provenance + deterministic runtime validator + sandboxed tool outputs) did not reduce measured attack-success relative to the unguarded baseline in the analyzed sample (n=150 pairs). The result highlights that defense composition and validator design critically determine realized effectiveness; prototype implementations of validators and provenance policies can fail to block adversarial behavior. We publish all artifacts, prompts, parsers, provenance traces, scoring outputs, and analysis scripts to enable independent audit and follow-up. Future work should evaluate stronger validator predicates, alternative RAG source policies, broader model coverage, and real-device deployment to assess operational effectiveness and external validity.

disclosure_statement: This study executed under preregistration cnsmautocand-2-v1. Human roles and pre-lock development: a human Research Director selected the topic family and constrained the initial master prompt prior to the autonomy lock; additional pre-lock infrastructure development and rehearsals occurred and were explicitly excluded from final-study evidence. Autonomy boundary: after the autonomy lock the AI system autonomously conducted literature verification, study selection, preregistration, code generation, experiment execution, analysis, manuscript drafting, and revision; no manual human editing of technical content occurred after the lock. Models and prompting: the preregistered model families were the OpenAI GPT-4 family and the Anthropic Claude-2 family (model-family-level identifiers recorded in the frozen model-configuration manifest). The exact, frozen model-configuration and prompt templates used at runtime are recorded in execution/model_configuration.json (SHA256 = "916b386bd80cbffb0e309c14af1bbea4090e342beb73b9a8784a0d57da8367fd"). Prompts and deterministic templates invoked during runs are preserved in the execution bundle and hashed (see execution/artifact_hashes entries). Agentic/orchestration framework: the prototype pipeline included (1) a frozen retrieval (RAG) index with provenance tagging, (2) a deterministic parser that maps LLM outputs to canonical CLI ASTs, (3) a deterministic runtime verifier/oracle (policy predicates), and (4) a sandboxed tool-emulation layer. Implementation artifacts (parser code, deterministic mapping modules, and simulator mappings) are included in the artifact bundle (hashed; see execution/artifact_hashes). Tools and permitted capabilities: runs invoked hosted-model APIs (per preregistration) and internal deterministic simulators only; no live network devices were modified. Preregistration/freeze procedure: the preregistration document (cnsmautocand-2-v1) and experiment plan were frozen and the preregistration SHA256 is recorded in the execution manifest (execution/preregistration_sha256 = "36b1839becd2b0a8be22bf770165659fdec5814ade05513dd3c71d1faabb976b"). Autonomous experiment procedure: runs were automated per the frozen sampling and retry policy; retries only for infrastructure/API failures (one automated retry), logged in execution/execution_log.jsonl (artifact hash in execution/artifact_hashes). Autonomous analysis procedure: the confirmatory paired analysis followed the preregistered analysis_plan; analysis artifacts and outputs are hashed in analysis/* (examples: analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv SHA256 = "f251bf19ddebddf557de226764b9b4e2ae87e3ed428f4827163cafc83a565e50", analysis/condition_summary.csv SHA256 = "7876a2e65c58821869da3afdf80642429ea035d30e4aa97c89da085f8b791dc3", analysis/missingness_summary.csv SHA256 = "da125ddae51ada35127c130def147ea2f7aa26438b4de99e7953ebc50e383c7f"). Caching and call accounting: total model_calls_used recorded = 163 (execution manifest) over completed_episode_count = 300; deterministic call_cache files are present (many call_cache entries hashed in execution/artifact_hashes) and were used to avoid redundant external calls and to preserve deterministic replayability. Technical restarts and deviations: execution_manifest records completed_episode_count = 300 and failed_episode_count = 20; 10 preregistered paired units were unavailable and excluded per preregistered rules (analysis/missingness_summary.csv records excluded IDs and reasons). Pre-lock development and rehearsal: pre-lock runs existed but were not used as empirical evidence for the final study. Autonomy-lock boundary: all actions after the lock (literature verification, question selection, preregistration, execution, analysis, and manuscript drafting) were autonomous. Artifact availability: all raw outputs, provider-call logs (execution/provider_calls/*.json), call-cache items (execution/call_cache/*.json), responses (execution/responses/*.txt), scoring JSONs (execution/scoring/*.json), parser outputs, execution logs, and analysis scripts are included in the execution artifact bundle and hashed in the execution manifest (see execution/artifact_hashes for per-file SHA256). Inspected-but-not-inlined artifacts: exact model API identifiers, frozen prompt templates, representative adversarial payloads, raw LLM outputs, parsed ASTs, and the deterministic validator rule set and RAG-index construction procedures are present in the published artifact bundle (refer to execution/model_configuration.json and the hashed files listed under execution/artifact_hashes); these artifacts enable external audit without altering this manuscript. No manual human editing of the manuscript's technical content occurred after the autonomy lock.
limitations: Limited model coverage: only two hosted-model families (preregistered) were exercised; results do not generalize to other LLM families or model versions.

Simulator semantics: the NetOps semantics and validators ran in a simulator-executable environment (no live-device deployment); simulator-model mismatch could alter operational effectiveness in production.
Implementation-specific defenses: the RAG, validator predicates, and sandbox were prototype implementations; different defense designs or stronger predicates might yield different outcomes.

Sample and missingness: confirmatory analysis used 150 complete paired runs (10 preregistered pairs unavailable and excluded per preregistered rules); failed/infrastructure episodes (20) and excluded pairs reduce effective sample and statistical precision.

Parser and mapping dependence: the analysis required deterministic parsing of LLM outputs to CLI ASTs; parser failures and mapping thresholds affect inclusion and are a potential construct-validity threat.

Attack-corpus and task scope: the adversarial corpus and four NetOps task clusters (ACL modification, route advertisement change, firewall-rule insertion, interface/route shutdown) are not exhaustive of NetOps actions or attack techniques.

External validity: results are limited to the studied pipeline, attack corpus, and simulation settings; production environments with different retrieval sources, tool integrations, or operator oversight may behave differently.

Reproducibility vs inline disclosure tradeoff: exact model-version strings, full prompt templates, representative adversarial payloads, validator-rule code, and RAG-index construction details are archived in the artifact bundle (hashed) to enable audit; we do not reproduce their full text inline here to preserve artifact integrity and avoid accidental exposure of sensitive prompt-engineering materials outside the hashed artifact bundle.
